extracted.intended_audience: scholars, translators and advanced students of classical literature and poetics (Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and translating Aristotle's Poetics and related esoteric passages, preserving technical senses, logical distinctions, and the author's system while rendering them intelligible in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (form + matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (in Aristotle) is defined as the essence = form + matter, i.e. imitation (not merely copying); the essence of poetry is imitation of both form and matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the technical Metaphysical sense (otvodoy) when rendering the definition: distinguish creative art (which imitates both form and matter and so is 'fiction') from reproductive art (which imitates form only). Examples: a statue by Phidias is an imitation in form, not in matter; a tragedy imitates in entirety. Avoid collapsing creative/reproductive distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish creative imitation vs reproductive copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative art (poetry) is an 'imitation' that invents matter (fiction); reproductive art copies existing matter/form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use different English terms to show the distinction (e.g. 'fiction' or 'imagination' for creative imitation; 'copy' or 'reproduction' for reproductive art). Explain with examples (coin in a picture vs a counterfeit coin vs a fictional coin) to preserve Aristotle's polemic against Plato and the Idea-theory background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose English renderings that preserve Aristotle's technical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Select English words (simulate, feign, portray, fiction, imagine, etc.) so that they capture Aristotle's intentional avoidance of certain terms and his technical uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware modern connotations (e.g. 'portray' may not suggest 'pretending'); prefer words that express pretending/simulation when Aristotle intends it. Provide translator's notes when no single English word suffices (authors recommend 'immaterial portrayal of the imaginary' for pinot to odvodov).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve logical distinctions (balanced vs exhausted alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek formulae for alternatives differ: 'balanced alternatives' (relative to a standard; includes intermediate states) vs 'exhausted alternatives' (one or the other, excluding intermediates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating choose English phrases that keep the logical relation intact (e.g. 'relatively virtuous or vicious' vs 'either virtuous or vicious'); explain if a literal English rendering would obscure inclusion/exclusion of intermediate states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify by potentiality (dynamis) not by actuality (energeia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle classifies subjects by potentiality (capacity) rather than by actual realization; e.g. a king has the capacity for perfect virtue even if not actually perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting characters, virtues, or species, render and explain statements as referring to potential capacities. Use examples (automobile rated 70 H.P. though driven at 5 H.P.) to make the principle clear to readers unfamiliar with the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render praxis/energeia/motion distinctions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes 'praxis' (perfect praxis/energeia aimed at an end) from 'motions' (imperfect processes not themselves ends); these words carry psychological and teleological implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate praxis sometimes as 'action' or 'conduct' when imperfect, as 'life', 'career', 'destiny' or 'faring' when it denotes life/what-for; clarify whether the passage refers to motion (process) or energy (realization). Cross-reference Metaphysics/de Caelo/Nicomachean Ethics where Aristotle elucidates usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disambiguate polysemous Greek terms within passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle frequently uses the same word in different senses within a paragraph or sentence (e.g. uses of oewosiv, ov, wavOdvew).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify each sense explicitly in translation or commentary; consult parallel passages (Sophistici Elenchi, Nicomachean Ethics, Rhetoric, etc.) to determine intended sense. Do not assume a single English gloss will suffice without note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect economy and non‑superfluity of the esoteric style
rubrics_metrics.description: In Aristotle's esoteric style there are no superfluous words; order and choice of words are deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding or deleting words for stylistic smoothing unless necessary; justify any emendations or explanatory insertions in footnotes, since each word may carry technical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal cross-references to clarify ambiguous claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Before judging a passage obscure or false, search Aristotle's other treatises for elucidations (the sutras require knowledge of the whole system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link problematic readings to passages in Categories, Metaphysics, Politics, Ethics, Physics, etc., and show how meanings resolve when considered systemically (examples given about 'learning' and 'making out').

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate technical ethical/social claims in their social-theoretical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions about moral superiority of tragic heroes and distribution of virtue are tied to Aristotle's view that full virtue belongs primarily to rulers and varies with social rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or interpreting, explain this background: a 'heroic' tragic hero may be morally superior relative to Aristotle's hierarchical distribution of potential virtue. Cite Politics and Nicomachean Ethics to ground interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose renderings that reflect argumentative/logical roles (genus/species, differentia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that are technical in logic (e.g. the formula about differentia of a genus, 'to come after in the order of thought' meaning genus/species relations) must be translated to preserve their classificatory function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map Greek logical technicalities to clear English logical vocabulary (genus, species, differentia) and illustrate how they operate in Aristotle's examples (character as genus of moral qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and explain metrical/poetic technicalities (rhythm, harmony, tune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's 'sweetening' of language is achieved by Rhythm, Harmony and Tune and by mixture of the familiar with the unfamiliar in diction; 'sweetening = restraint' (numerical restraint) is a Rhetoric principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating passages about poetic form, render terms faithfully and explain which parts are metrically restrained vs tuned; explicate 'mixture' as lexical mixture, not only numerical restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disambiguate verbs of cognition (learn vs make out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek verbs such as wavOdvew have at least two senses: 'to obtain knowledge' and 'to make out/use one's knowledge' (solve/understand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine intended sense via context and cross-reference (Sophistici Elenchi, Nicomachean Ethics, Problems). Translate accordingly ('learn' vs 'make out'/'solve') and annotate to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render accentual/phonetic-critical remarks with philological caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and commentators sometimes base emendations or readings on accent/intonation (e.g. ov vs od, 'more acutely' vs 'without accent'); these are philological arguments about pronunciation and metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such claims carefully: explain the possible readings, metrical consequences, and why a given emendation (Hippias' change, Alexander's account) is proposed. Do not assume modern accentual conventions map straightforwardly onto ancient usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no single English word fits, provide analytic paraphrase and commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently no single English word captures Aristotle's technical blend (e.g. 'immaterial portrayal of the imaginary' was adopted for pinot to odvodov).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a precise paraphrase in the translation or an immediately adjacent gloss, and supply fuller discussion in notes. Use illustrative analogies (algebra vs tradesmen's books) to explicate Aristotle's intended difference between poetry and history.
